passage: In the courtyard of their house in the small town, Chetan waited until his mother Leela had finished her evening prayers. Then he sat on the step below her, the way he had as a boy. "Amma, I've decided something. I'm taking the job at the dairy cooperative in the next town. It starts in June." Leela's hands stopped on her beads. "You didn't ask Appa." "I'm telling you both first, before anyone else. I thought about it for months. I'll be home every Saturday, and I'll still do the accounts for Appa's shop on Sundays." She was quiet a long time. "Your Appa decided everything himself at your age too," she said finally. "He also forgot to call." Chetan grinned. "I won't forget. You can check." She pressed his head once, lightly, and went in to tell her husband.

qa.q: Where is Chetan's new job?
qa.a: At the dairy cooperative in the next town.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when her hands stopped on her beads?
qa.a: She was surprised and a little hurt that Chetan hadn't asked Appa, sensing the family's usual order shifting.

qa.q: How did Chetan make his decision feel respectful rather than defiant?
qa.a: He told them first, sat below her as he used to, and offered concrete ways to stay close: Saturdays at home and Sunday accounts.

qa.q: How might Appa react when Leela tells him?
qa.a: He may be startled not to have been asked, but Leela's calm and the Sunday accounts could help him see his son's respect.

subtype: Becoming an adult who is also a family member [Response]
passage: Every second Sunday, Felix took the train from Berlin to his parents' house outside Hamburg for lunch. This time he brought Aiko. Over potato salad he said, "Mama, Papa, I wanted to tell you in person. Aiko's been offered a research post in Osaka, and I'm going with her. I've arranged to work remotely for my firm." His father set down his fork. "You've decided." "We have. I'm not asking you to approve it. I'm asking you to be part of it." Felix slid a printed calendar across the table. "Video call every other Sunday, same time as these lunches. And we've booked flights home for Christmas." His mother looked at Aiko, then at the calendar. "You were always the one who needed a plan," she said, and pinned it to the fridge.

qa.q: Where has Aiko been offered a research post?
qa.a: In Osaka.

qa.q: What might Felix's father be feeling when he sets down his fork?
qa.a: He may feel surprised and a little shut out, realising the decision was made without him.

qa.q: Why was bringing a printed calendar a good choice?
qa.a: It showed Felix planned to keep regular contact, so his parents could feel included rather than left behind.

qa.q: What does Felix's mother pinning the calendar to the fridge suggest about how she sees the move?
qa.a: She seems to accept it and wants to stay part of their life, trusting Felix as an adult who plans 🙂

grounding: A young man tells his parents in person about his decision to move abroad, invites them in rather than asking permission, and sets up regular contact.

passage:
In the canteen of the Pune software park, Gautam, twenty-five, finished his lunch and called his mother before he lost his nerve.
"Ma, I wanted you to hear it from me. I've accepted the offer from the solar company in Jaipur. I start in June."
Hansa was quiet on the line. "You didn't ask us."
"I didn't ask, Ma, because it's my decision. But I wanted to tell you before anyone else, and explain why." He told her about the work, the team, the rent he had checked. "And I'll call every Sunday, same as now. You and Papa come in winter; I'll show you the fort."
"And if Papa is upset?"
"Then I'll call him tonight and listen. I'm not doing this to fight him."
A long breath. "Send me the address, beta."
Gautam sent it before his lunch break ended, and his hands were steady.

qa.q: Where is the solar company Gautam will join?
qa.a: It is in Jaipur.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she said 'You didn't ask us'?
qa.a: She felt a little hurt and left out, used to being asked rather than told.

qa.q: How did Gautam avoid both asking permission and defiance?
qa.a: He told his mother warmly and first, explained his reasons, promised Sunday calls, and offered to listen to Papa rather than fight.

qa.q: What might 'Send me the address, beta' show about Hansa's shift?
qa.a: It shows she is moving from expecting obedience to accepting his choice with respect and care.

grounding: A young man tells his mother about his own job decision with warmth rather than asking permission or defying, and keeps up regular contact.

passage:
Dear Ma and Papa,
I'm writing because on the phone I either talk too fast or cry, and I want to say this properly.
I've decided to marry Sameer. We've been together two years, and you've met him twice at Yamini Didi's. I'm not asking your permission; I'm twenty-five and this is my choice. But I don't want to announce it like a news item either. You are my family, and I want you in it.
I know Papa had hoped for someone from our own circle, and I understand that hurts. I'd like to come home next weekend with Sameer, so you can ask him anything you want, and I'll listen too.
Whatever you feel, I'll still call every evening at nine, and I'll still come for Ma's birthday.
With love, and a bit nervous,
Parveen

qa.q: Where have Ma and Papa met Sameer before?
qa.a: Twice, at Yamini Didi's.

qa.q: What does Parveen mean by not wanting to announce it like a news item?
qa.a: Parveen wants to make this choice independently but still feels close to Ma and Papa and wants them included warmly, not shut out.

qa.q: What steps does Parveen offer to keep the relationship strong while deciding independently?
qa.a: Bringing Sameer home to answer questions, listening to them too, and keeping the nine o'clock calls and Ma's birthday visit.

qa.q: How might Papa feel reading this letter?
qa.a: He may feel hurt that his hopes weren't met, but also respected, since Parveen explains with care and invites him to talk.

grounding: A young adult informs parents of a marriage decision with warmth instead of asking permission or defying them, and promises regular contact.
